c: A motor is not an LED

A microcontroller pin can supply perhaps 20 milliamps. A small hobby motor draws a few hundred milliamps while spinning freely and several times that at the moment it starts or when it is held still, which is called the stall current. Connecting a motor directly to a pin will not turn it and may damage the pin. The pin's job is to control a switch, and the switch carries the motor current from a separate supply. A motor is also a coil of wire, and coils store energy in their magnetic field. That stored energy is the second problem to solve.
One direction with one transistor

For a motor that only runs one way, use an N-channel MOSFET of the kind described as logic level, which turns fully on with 3.3 or 5 volts at its gate. Connect the motor between the positive supply and the transistor's drain, and the source to ground. Drive the gate from the microcontroller through a resistor of about 100 ohms. Add a 10 kilohm resistor from gate to ground, so the transistor stays off while the microcontroller is starting up and its pins are floating. The grounds of the motor supply and the microcontroller must be joined.
The diode you must not leave out

Current in a coil cannot stop instantly. When the transistor switches off, the motor's inductance keeps pushing current and the voltage at the drain leaps upward until something gives way, often the transistor. The fix is one diode connected across the motor, pointing against the normal flow, with its striped end to the positive supply. In normal running it does nothing. At switch-off it gives the coil current a loop to circulate in and die away harmlessly. A fast Schottky diode such as the 1N5819 suits small motors. This part is called a flyback diode.
Speed by switching fast

Speed is controlled by switching the transistor on and off rapidly and varying the fraction of time it is on. At half the time on, a 12 volt motor behaves roughly as if it were fed 6 volts. The motor's own inertia and inductance smooth out the pulses. Switching at a few thousand times a second works but can produce an audible whine from the windings. Switching above about 20,000 times a second moves the noise out of hearing. Very low duty will not start a motor from rest, since it needs a certain push to overcome friction.
Reversing: the H-bridge

To reverse a DC motor you must swap the polarity across it. An H-bridge does that with four switches arranged like the letter H, with the motor as the crossbar. Close the top left and bottom right switches and current flows through the motor one way. Close the top right and bottom left and it flows the other way. Close both bottom switches and the motor's terminals are shorted together, which brakes it firmly, because a spinning motor is a generator. Open all four and it coasts to a stop.
The forbidden state

There is one combination that must never happen. If the top and bottom switches on the same side are both closed, they form a short circuit straight across the power supply. This is called shoot-through, and it destroys transistors in an instant. It can occur for a few millionths of a second during every reversal if the timing is careless. Driver chips handle this internally, which is the main reason to buy one. The old L298 works but can lose around 2 volts or more in its transistors. Modern MOSFET drivers such as the TB6612FNG and DRV8833 lose far less.
Sizing and wiring

Choose the driver for the stall current, not the running current. You can estimate stall current by measuring the motor's winding resistance with a multimeter. A 12 volt motor that reads 6 ohms will draw about 2 amps at stall. Give the motors their own supply where you can, and put a capacitor of a few hundred microfarads near the driver, because the surge at start-up can dip the supply enough to reset a microcontroller. A 100 nanofarad ceramic capacitor soldered across the motor terminals cuts the electrical noise from the brushes.
What is in the tank

Lift the lid of the tank and set it somewhere safe, since it is heavy and brittle. The water in the tank is clean. You will see four things. A rubber flap at the bottom covers the outlet to the bowl. This is the flapper. A chain links it to the flush handle. A tall valve at one side refills the tank after a flush, controlled by a float that rises with the water. And an open vertical pipe, the overflow tube, stands in the middle to carry away water if the tank overfills.
How a flush works

Pressing the handle lifts the flapper by its chain. The tank's water rushes down into the bowl and pushes the contents over the bend in the drain. As the tank empties, the flapper drops back onto its seat and seals. The float has fallen with the water, which opens the fill valve, and the tank refills until the float rises far enough to shut the valve. A toilet runs on when one of those two seals fails. Either the flapper is letting water out, or the fill valve is not shutting off.
Finding which one

Look at the water level first. If water is spilling into the top of the overflow tube, the fill valve is the problem, since it is filling too high or not closing. If the level sits below the top of the tube, test the flapper. Put a few drops of food colouring in the tank and do not flush for fifteen minutes. If colour shows up in the bowl, water is leaking past the flapper. A toilet that refills briefly every so often with nobody near it is doing this.
Replacing the flapper

Turn off the water at the small valve on the wall or floor behind the toilet, then flush to empty the tank. Unhook the chain from the handle arm and unclip the flapper from the pegs on the overflow tube. Take it with you to the hardware shop, because flappers come in two common sizes and several fittings. Before fitting the new one, wipe the rim it sits on to remove any slime or mineral crust. Clip it on, hook the chain, turn the water on and test.
Getting the chain right

The chain needs a little slack, about a centimetre. Too tight and it holds the flapper slightly open, so the toilet runs. Too loose and the handle will not lift the flapper far enough for a full flush, or the spare chain can fall under the flapper and stop it sealing. Trim off any long tail of chain. Flush several times and watch the flapper drop and seat each time. This small adjustment cures many toilets on its own.
The fill valve

If the water was running into the overflow tube, lower the water level. Most modern fill valves have a screw or a sliding clip on the float for this. Set the level about 2 or 3 centimetres below the top of the tube. If the valve will not shut off at any setting, or hisses constantly, replace it. With the water off and the tank empty, undo the supply connection and the large nut under the tank, lift the old valve out and fit the new one following its instructions. Tighten plastic nuts by hand.
When to call a plumber

These repairs need no special tools and the parts are inexpensive. Some problems are not for a first attempt. Water appearing around the base of the toilet points to the seal between the toilet and the drain. A crack in the tank or bowl means replacement. And if the shut-off valve on the wall will not turn, or drips once you have turned it, leave it and have it replaced, since forcing an old valve can start a leak you cannot stop without closing the main.
What an apology is for

An apology does a specific job. Someone has been wronged, and they need to know three things: that you understand what you did, that you accept it was your doing, and that it is less likely to happen again. Regret alone does not deliver those. Many apologies fail because they are aimed at ending the speaker's discomfort or closing the subject. The test of an apology is whether the other person ends up feeling understood, not whether you feel you have said sorry.
Name what you did

Begin with the specific act. Say that you are sorry you missed the deadline you had promised and left them to explain it to the client. Do not say that you are sorry about what happened. Vague apologies sound like guesses, and they leave the other person wondering whether you know what the problem was. Being specific costs something, because it means saying the unflattering thing aloud. That cost is part of what makes the apology believable.
Own it without the escape hatches

Three small phrases ruin apologies. The word if, as in sorry if anyone was offended, questions whether anything happened. The word but, as in sorry, but I was under pressure, cancels what came before it. And the passive voice, as in mistakes were made, removes the person who made them. Say I did this. Explanations are not forbidden. They belong later, and only if asked for or useful, and they must not be offered as a reason the other person should not mind.
Acknowledge the effect

Say what your action cost them, in their terms. You were embarrassed in front of your team. You had to stay late to fix it. You stopped being able to rely on what I told you. This is the part most often left out, and it is the part the listener is waiting for. If you do not know how it affected them, ask, and then listen without defending yourself. Being told the impact is uncomfortable. Sitting through it is evidence that you take it seriously.
Repair and commit

Then say what you will do. Where the damage can be mended, offer to mend it: redo the work, replace the thing, correct the record with the people who heard the wrong version. Where it cannot, say what will be different. A specific change is worth more than a promise to do better. From now on I will send you the draft two days ahead is something they can check. Do not promise what you may not deliver, since a broken commitment made during an apology is worse than none.
Timing and manner

Apologise soon, though not so fast that you have not understood what you are apologising for. For anything serious, do it in person or by voice, where your tone can be heard. Keep it short. A long apology starts to be about you and your feelings. Do not ask for forgiveness on the spot or expect the mood to lift at once. The other person is entitled to stay annoyed for a while. Having apologised, do not bring it up again to check whether you are forgiven.
Receiving one

Two things help when you are on the other side. If the apology is real, say so plainly, with thanks. You need not say it is fine when it is not. Thank you, I appreciate you saying that is enough. If the apology is hollow, you can accept the gesture and still name what is missing, for instance that you would like to know it will not happen again. And judge the apology finally by what follows. The words open the door. The changed behaviour is the apology being kept.
Movement sends a message

The other side cannot see your limit. They infer it from how you behave, and above all from how you give ground. A large, quick concession tells them your opening was padded and there is more to come. A small, slow one tells them you are near the end. This means the pattern of your concessions is information you are handing over whether you intend it or not. Planning that pattern before you sit down is as much a part of preparing as knowing your walk-away point.
Trade, do not give

The first rule is that nothing moves for free. When you give something, ask for something in the same sentence. If they want delivery two weeks sooner, the reply is that you can do that if they confirm the order by Friday. A concession with a condition attached is a trade. A concession with nothing attached is a gift, and gifts in a negotiation are rarely answered in kind. They are more often taken as a sign that pressing harder will produce another one.
Make each step smaller

Suppose you are selling and have 1,000 dollars of room. Giving it in steps of 500, then 300, then 150, then 50 signals that you are running out and the end is near. Giving it as four steps of 250 signals nothing, and the buyer will simply ask for a fifth. Giving 50, then 150, then 300, then 500 teaches the buyer that waiting pays. The total given is the same in all three. Only the shrinking pattern leads the other side to conclude, without being told, that they have reached the floor.
Give what is cheap to you

The best concessions cost you little and are worth a lot to the other party. A supplier with spare capacity can offer fast delivery at almost no cost. A buyer with cash can offer quick payment. An employer who cannot raise a salary can sometimes offer a day at home or an earlier review. Before negotiating, list everything that could be varied besides the price, and mark what each item costs you. Then ask questions to learn what the other side values. Trades across different items are where both sides gain.
Name what you are giving up

A concession the other side does not notice earns nothing. Say what it is and what it costs you. This is not a matter of theatre. People value what they are told has value, and a move made silently is often treated as the correction of an inflated opening. Compare two replies. One is fine, 9,500. The other is that 9,500 is below what you had planned for, and you can do it if the contract runs for two years. The second reply marks the movement and asks for a return.
Do not bid against yourself

If you have made an offer and the other side has only said it is too high, do not improve it. Ask for their figure. Making two moves in a row without a move from them means you are negotiating against yourself, and they have learned that saying no is enough to produce a better offer. The same applies to silence. After you state your position, stop talking. The urge to fill a pause with a sweetener is strong, and the pause is frequently just the other person thinking.
Before the next one

Write down four things in advance. Your opening position and your walk-away point. The list of items you can vary, with their cost to you. What you will ask for in exchange for each. And the size of your steps, largest first. Then keep a simple record during the talks of what each side has given. It keeps you from conceding twice on the same point, and it lets you say with accuracy that you have moved three times and they have moved once.
The setup

Three players are left in a small tournament. The prize pool is 1,000 dollars, paid 500 for first, 300 for second and 200 for third. The stacks are 5,000 chips for player A, 3,000 for player B and 2,000 for player C. Everyone is already sure of 200. The question the independent chip model answers is how much each stack is worth right now, on average, if the players are of equal skill. The model makes one assumption. Your chance of finishing first equals your share of the chips.
First place

Start with first place, which is the easy part. Player A has half the chips and so wins half the time. Player B wins 30 percent of the time and player C 20 percent. If the tournament paid everything to the winner, the calculation would stop here and each chip would be worth the same amount of money. It does not stop here, because second and third place also pay, and a player with few chips collects those prizes more often than chip counts alone suggest.
Second place for the leader

To find how often A finishes second, imagine each rival winning in turn. If B wins, which happens 30 percent of the time, remove B's chips. A then has 5,000 of the remaining 7,000, so A takes second about 71 percent of those times. If C wins, 20 percent of the time, A has 5,000 of the remaining 8,000, and takes second 62.5 percent of those times. Added together, A finishes second about 34 percent of the time. First is 50 percent, so third must be the remaining 16 percent.
The money

Now multiply. For player A, 50 percent of 500 is 250. About 34 percent of 300 is 102. About 16 percent of 200 is 32. Player A's stack is worth about 384 dollars. The same working gives about 328 dollars for B and about 289 for C, and the three figures add up to the 1,000 in the pool. Look at what happened. A holds half the chips but only 38 percent of the money. C holds a fifth of the chips and 29 percent of the money.
Why chips lose value as you gain them

Suppose C doubles up through B, so the stacks become 5,000 for A, 1,000 for B and 4,000 for C. Run the sum again and C's stack is worth about 364 dollars. C doubled in chips, from 2,000 to 4,000, but rose in money only from 289 to 364, a gain of about 76 dollars. Had C lost the same pot, C would be out in third with 200, a loss of about 89 dollars. The same number of chips is worth more when lost than when won.
What that does to a call

Say B moves all in and C must decide whether to call for the whole stack. Ignore the blinds to keep it simple. In chips, C risks 2,000 to win 2,000 and needs to win half the time. In money, C risks 89 dollars to gain 76. Divide 89 by the sum of the two, 165, and C needs to win about 54 percent of the time. Those extra four points are sometimes called a risk premium. With more players left and bigger jumps between prizes, the premium can be several times larger.
Using it at the table

Nobody does this arithmetic during a hand, and software does it instantly for study afterwards. What you carry to the table is the shape of the result. Calling an all-in for your tournament life requires a better hand than the pot odds alone suggest. Moving all in yourself is more attractive than calling, because your opponents face the same penalty for calling you. Big stacks can lean on middle stacks, who have the most to lose. And far from the money, the effect is small enough to ignore.
The surprise

Ask how many people must be in a room before there is an even chance that two of them share a birthday, and most guesses land well above 100. With 365 days to choose from, it feels as though you would need about half that many people. The answer is 23. With 23 people the chance of at least one shared birthday is 50.7 percent. With 30 it is about 71 percent. With 50 it is 97 percent, and with 70 it is 99.9 percent.
Pairs, not people

Intuition goes wrong because it imagines one person comparing their own birthday with everyone else's. That gives only 22 comparisons in a group of 23. But the question is whether any two people match. The first person can pair with 22 others, the second with 21 more, and so on. That makes 253 different pairs. Each pair has a 1 in 365 chance of matching. With 253 chances at a rare event, a hit somewhere becomes likely. The number of pairs grows roughly with the square of the group size.
The calculation

The clean way to work it out is to find the chance that nobody matches and subtract from 1. The second person avoids the first person's birthday with probability 364 over 365. The third avoids both with probability 363 over 365. Keep multiplying. By the twenty-third person the fraction is 343 over 365, and the product of all 22 fractions is about 0.493. So the chance that all 23 birthdays differ is 49.3 percent, and the chance that at least two coincide is 50.7 percent.
A different question

Do not confuse this with the chance that someone shares your birthday. That is a much rarer event, because only the pairs that include you count. In a room of 23 it is about 6 percent. To reach an even chance that someone matches your own birthday, you need 253 other people. The gap between those two questions, any match versus a particular match, explains a great deal about why coincidences feel more miraculous than they are.
Coincidences in general

You notice the coincidence that happened. You do not count the thousands of possible coincidences that did not. Meeting a neighbour in a foreign airport seems astonishing. But you would have been equally astonished to meet any one of hundreds of acquaintances, in any of dozens of places, in any year. Add up all the pairs and the event stops being unlikely. With enough people and enough chances, it would be strange if nothing strange occurred. A lottery drawing the same numbers twice is this effect at work.
Why programmers care

The same arithmetic matters in computing. Programs often give each file or password a short fingerprint called a hash. Two different inputs with the same hash are a collision, and it is tempting to think collisions are negligible if there are billions of possible values. The birthday sum says otherwise. An even chance of a collision arrives after about 1.2 times the square root of the number of possible values. For 365 days that gives about 23. For a hash with about 4 billion possible values, it gives only about 77,000 items.
The lesson to keep

When you estimate the chance of a coincidence, count the opportunities for it honestly. Ask how many pairs, how many days, how many people could have produced something you would have found equally striking. A one in a million event happens many times a day in a large country. The birthday problem is a small, checkable example of a large point. Your sense of what is unlikely is tuned to yourself, and the world runs on all the pairs at once.
No pressure needed

The glass on a phone has no moving parts and does not respond to force. It senses the electrical effect of a finger. Older touch panels, the resistive kind still found on some industrial equipment, worked by pressure. Two flexible conductive layers were pushed together and the contact point was measured. They needed a firm press and could track only one point reliably. The capacitive screens that became standard on phones in the late 2000s respond to the lightest contact, track many fingers at once and sit behind hard glass that does not wear out.
A grid of capacitors

Behind the cover glass are two layers of electrodes, one running in rows and one in columns, separated by a thin insulator. They are made of indium tin oxide, a material that conducts electricity and is nearly transparent in a thin film. Wherever a row crosses a column, the two conductors and the insulator between them form a very small capacitor. A phone screen might have 15 columns and 30 rows, which makes 450 crossings. The electrodes are often shaped as chains of diamonds so that the electric field spreads up through the glass.
What a finger changes

Your body conducts electricity and is very large compared with the electrodes. When a fingertip comes close to a crossing, some of the electric field that linked the row to the column ends on the finger instead. Less charge passes between that row and column, so the capacitance at the crossing falls slightly. The change is tiny, a fraction of an already small value, but it is repeatable. Note that the finger does not need to touch a conductor. The effect passes through the glass, which is why a screen works through a thin protector.
Scanning the grid

A controller chip measures every crossing in turn. It sends a signal down one row and measures how much of it arrives on each column. Then it moves to the next row. One complete pass over the grid produces a table of numbers, one per crossing, and the controller repeats the pass many times every second, commonly 60 times or more. It subtracts a stored baseline taken when nothing was touching. What remains is a picture of the screen in which each fingertip shows up as a small bump covering several neighbouring crossings.
Finer than the grid

The electrodes are spaced about 4 or 5 millimetres apart, yet a screen places your finger to a fraction of a millimetre. It does that by interpolation. A fingertip disturbs several crossings at once, and the controller calculates the centre of weight of the bump. Suppose three neighbouring columns show changes of 20, 60 and 40. The middle one is strongest, but the right one beats the left, so the centre lies a little to the right of the middle column, by about a sixth of the spacing. On a 5 millimetre grid that is under 1 millimetre.
Many fingers, gloves and water

Because each crossing is measured separately, two fingers make two separate bumps, and pinching and rotating gestures follow directly. Ordinary gloves fail because they hold the finger too far from the glass and do not conduct. Gloves made for screens have conductive thread in the fingertips. Water is the awkward case. A droplet conducts, links neighbouring electrodes and can look like a touch, which is why a wet screen behaves erratically. Controllers use extra measurements to tell a grounded finger from a floating droplet, with partial success.
Build a touch button

The same idea works on a bench. A touch button is a copper pad on a circuit board, covered by plastic or glass, wired to a microcontroller pin. The microcontroller measures how long the pad takes to charge. A nearby finger adds a few picofarads and the time grows. Some microcontrollers, the ESP32 among them, have pins with this measurement built in. The code that makes it reliable keeps a slowly moving baseline, so drift from temperature and humidity is ignored, and reports a touch only when the reading departs from that baseline by a set margin.
Get somewhere safe

A flat tyre does not have to be changed where it happened. Slow down, put your hazard lights on, and drive gently to a place that is flat, firm and well away from moving traffic, such as a car park or a quiet side road. Driving a short distance on a flat may ruin the tyre, and that is cheaper than being struck by a passing vehicle. On the shoulder of a fast road, the safer choice is often to get everyone out and behind the barrier, and call for roadside help.
Set up before you lift

Apply the parking brake firmly. Put an automatic in park and a manual in first gear or reverse. If you have a wedge, a brick or a large stone, place it against the wheel diagonally opposite the flat. Get passengers out of the car and off the road. Then find the spare wheel, the jack and the wheel wrench, which are usually under the boot floor. If the car has locking wheel nuts, you will need the special key, often kept with the jack or in the glovebox.
Loosen first, then lift

Loosen the wheel nuts before raising the car, while the tyre's grip on the ground stops the wheel from turning. Give each nut about half a turn anticlockwise. They can be very tight, and using your foot on the wrench is acceptable. Then find the jacking point nearest the flat. The handbook shows it, and there is often a notch or mark on the seam under the sill. A jack placed anywhere else can bend the floor or slip. Raise the car until the flat tyre is just clear of the ground.
Never get under it

The jack supplied with a car is designed only to hold it up long enough to change a wheel. It can tip or sink into soft ground. Do not put any part of your body under the car while it is on the jack. A simple precaution is to slide the spare wheel under the sill beside the jack before you take the flat off, and then slide the flat there in its place. If the jack fails, the car lands on the wheel and not on the brake disc or on you.
Swap the wheel

Remove the loosened nuts and keep them together where they cannot roll away. Pull the wheel straight towards you and off. Lift the spare onto the hub, lining up the holes, and screw the nuts on by hand until they are snug. Tighten them in a criss-cross order, moving to the nut opposite each time and not around the circle. This draws the wheel on evenly. Do not apply full force yet, since pushing hard on a raised car can rock it off the jack.
Lower and tighten

Lower the car until the tyre is carrying weight, then tighten the nuts firmly with the wrench, again in the criss-cross order. Go around twice. Stow the flat, the jack and the tools so they cannot fly about. The handbook gives a tightening figure for the nuts, and a garage can check it with a torque wrench. It is widely advised to recheck the nuts after the first 50 miles or so, because they can settle.
After the change

Many spares are narrow temporary wheels. They carry a speed limit, commonly 50 miles an hour, printed on the wheel, and they are meant to get you to a tyre shop and no further. Check the spare's pressure a few times a year, since a spare is often found flat on the day it is needed. Some cars carry no spare at all, only a bottle of sealant and a compressor. That kit can seal a small hole in the tread and will not help with a damaged sidewall, so know which your car has before you need it.
The rule

William of Ockham was an English friar and philosopher of the fourteenth century. The principle that carries his name, in a common wording, says that entities should not be multiplied beyond necessity. In plain terms, do not assume more than you need to. If two explanations account for the same facts equally well, prefer the one with fewer moving parts. The razor is the image of shaving off assumptions that do no work. Ockham did not invent the idea, and versions appear as far back as Aristotle, but he used it so often that it took his name.
Why simpler is likelier

There is arithmetic behind the preference. Every extra assumption is another thing that has to be true. Suppose an explanation needs four independent assumptions and each has an 80 percent chance of being right. The chance that all four hold is about 41 percent. A rival explanation needing one such assumption stands at 80 percent. Elaborate stories feel more convincing because they are detailed, but each detail is another place to be wrong. A chain of plausible steps can be an unlikely whole.
An everyday case

Your car will not start. One explanation is a flat battery. Another is that a fault in the engine computer has coincided with a failed fuel pump. Both fit the silence when you turn the key. The first needs one common failure. The second needs two rarer ones at once. The razor says to check the battery first. Mechanics, doctors and engineers work this way by training. A saying taught to medical students makes the same point: when you hear hoofbeats, think of horses before zebras.
A famous near miss

In 2011, physicists at an experiment called OPERA reported particles called neutrinos apparently arriving faster than light, which would have overturned a century of physics. The two candidate explanations were a revolution in the laws of nature or an undetected error in a very complicated measurement. Most physicists, including the team itself, bet on the error and asked others to help find it. The following year it was traced to faulty equipment, including a loose fibre-optic cable. The simpler explanation was duller and correct.
Simple does not mean easy

The razor is often misused to favour whichever explanation is easiest to state or most comfortable to believe. That is not what it says. The count that matters is of assumptions, not of words. It was magic is short and assumes a great deal. The razor also applies only among explanations that fit all the evidence. If the simple story leaves facts unexplained, it has not earned its place, and you must accept a more complicated one. A wise limit is to make things as simple as possible and no simpler.
When more than one thing is true

The world is not obliged to be simple. In medicine there is a counter-saying, known as Hickam's dictum, that a patient can have as many diseases as they please. An elderly patient with five symptoms may well have three conditions and not one rare disease that explains them all. Accidents and business failures usually have several causes acting together. So use the razor to decide the order in which to test ideas, and let the evidence decide which idea survives.
Using it

When you face a puzzle, write down the candidate explanations and under each list what would have to be true for it to hold. Count the items and judge how likely each one is. Test the leanest candidate first, in the cheapest way available. If it fails, move to the next. Be most suspicious of your own explanation when you notice yourself adding a new assumption each time a fact does not fit. An explanation that needs constant patching is telling you something.
The puzzle

It seems obvious that if you are better than someone else at two jobs, you should do both yourself. David Ricardo showed in 1817 that this is wrong, using an example of England and Portugal trading cloth and wine. What matters is not who is better in absolute terms. It is what each party gives up to produce a thing. Time spent on one task is time not spent on another, and the party who gives up least to make something has what economists call a comparative advantage in it.
Two producers

Take two countries with 100 days of labour each. In the first, a day makes 10 rolls of cloth or 5 barrels of wine. In the second, a day makes 2 rolls of cloth or 4 barrels of wine. The first is better at both. Now look at the cost of wine in each. In the first country, a barrel of wine means giving up 2 rolls of cloth. In the second, a barrel means giving up only half a roll. Wine is cheaper to make in the second country, measured in the cloth forgone.
Without trade

Suppose each country splits its time evenly. The first makes 500 rolls of cloth and 250 barrels of wine. The second makes 100 rolls and 200 barrels. Between them, the world has 600 rolls of cloth and 450 barrels of wine. Each country consumes exactly what it makes. Nothing is wrong with this arrangement, except that the same people working the same days could have more of both goods.
With specialisation

Let the second country make only wine, 400 barrels. Let the first spend 70 days on cloth and 30 on wine, making 700 rolls and 150 barrels. The world now has 700 rolls of cloth, up from 600, and 550 barrels of wine, up from 450. Nobody worked harder and nobody learned a new skill. The extra output came entirely from each country shifting towards the thing it gives up least to make.
Both sides gain

Now they trade 150 rolls of cloth for 150 barrels of wine. The first country ends up with 550 rolls and 300 barrels, against 500 and 250 before. The second ends up with 150 rolls and 250 barrels, against 100 and 200 before. Each has more of both. The price, one roll per barrel, works because it lies between the two countries' own costs. The first country would have to give up 2 rolls at home to get a barrel. The second gets a roll for 1 barrel that would cost it 2 at home.
The same thing at a desk

The principle applies to people. A lawyer who types faster than her assistant still gains by handing over the typing, because an hour of her typing costs an hour of legal work, and that is worth much more. A founder who can do the bookkeeping better than anyone should usually still not do it. When deciding what to delegate, do not ask whether you could do it better. Ask what else your time would produce, and hand over the tasks where the gap is smallest.
What it does not say

The result is about total gains, and it leaves real questions open. It does not say that everyone within a country gains. Cloth workers in the second country lose their work when it specialises in wine, and the gain to the whole is no comfort unless some of it reaches them. It assumes workers can move between industries, which takes time and sometimes never happens. And it describes a moment. Countries can and do change what they are good at through investment and learning.
The problem it solves

Imagine an opponent who knows you fold whenever you lack a strong hand. That opponent can bet every time with nothing and show a profit, because the pot they pick up when you fold outweighs what they lose when you happen to call. To stop this, you have to continue with enough hands that a bet with nothing merely breaks even. The share of your hands you must continue with is called the minimum defence frequency. It depends on one thing, the size of the bet compared with the pot.
The fraction

Divide the pot before the bet by the pot plus the bet. That is the share of your range that should call or raise. Facing a bet the size of the pot, the answer is one half. Facing half the pot, it is two thirds. Facing a third of the pot, it is three quarters. Facing twice the pot, it is one third. The pattern is easy to hold in mind. Small bets must be defended widely, and large bets allow you to fold most of what you hold.
Why it works

Look at it from the bluffer's side. Someone who bets 50 into a pot of 100 risks 50 to win 100. The bluff shows a profit if it works more than one time in three. So you must not fold more than one time in three, which means defending two thirds. For a pot-sized bet of 100, the bluffer risks 100 to win 100 and needs folds more than half the time, so you defend half. The defender's fraction and the bluffer's break-even point are the same sum seen from opposite seats.
It applies to ranges, not hands

The fraction says nothing about what to do with the two cards in front of you until you place them among all the hands you could hold in that spot. Suppose you reach the river and face a bet of half the pot. List the hands you could plausibly have, strongest to weakest. The top two thirds of that list continue. If your actual hand sits in the top two thirds, call. If it sits in the bottom third, fold without regret, even if it is a hand that looks pretty.
A worked example

You defended your big blind, called a bet on a flop of queen, eight, three, and both of you checked the turn. The river is a deuce and your opponent bets 60 into 80. The fraction is 80 divided by 140, or 57 percent. Your range here contains queens with various kickers, eights, pocket pairs between the eight and the queen, and a few missed hands. Queens and the better eights make up more than 57 percent of it. So a pair of eights with a good kicker calls, and a pair of fours folds.
Where it stops being right

The fraction is a defence against an opponent who bluffs as often as the theory allows. Many players do not. At low stakes, a large river bet from a cautious player is a real hand most of the time. Against that player, defending half your range to a pot-sized bet pays off strong hands again and again. Fold more. Against a player who fires at every checked pot, defend more than the fraction. It is a baseline that protects you against unknown opponents, and you should move away from it as you learn who you are playing.
What to take from it

Use the fraction in three ways. First, as a check on yourself. If you find you fold to nearly every bet on the turn and river, you are being robbed, and the sums say so. Second, as a guide when bluffing. A half-pot bluff needs to work a third of the time, so aim it at players who fold more than that. Third, as a reason to size your own bets with thought, since a large bet forces fewer calls from a correct defender, and a small one invites many.
Early estimates

In 1650 the scholar James Ussher added up the generations in scripture and dated creation to 4004 before Christ. By the nineteenth century, geologists looking at the thickness of rock layers and the slowness of erosion were sure the Earth was vastly older, though they could not say by how much. The physicist Lord Kelvin tried a calculation. He assumed the planet began molten and worked out how long it would take to cool to its present state. His answers ranged from 20 million to a few hundred million years, and he came to favour the low end.
What Kelvin could not know

Kelvin's physics was sound and his assumptions were not. He did not know that the Earth has an internal source of heat. Radioactivity, discovered in 1896, keeps the interior warm, and slow churning in the mantle carries heat up from the depths. Either would upset his sum. Geologists and biologists had needed far more time than he allowed, and the discovery of radioactivity showed where it had been hiding. It also provided the tool that would settle the matter.
Atoms as clocks

A radioactive element decays into another at a fixed pace, set by its half-life, the time for half of any sample to change. Uranium 238 decays through a chain of steps into lead 206 with a half-life of about 4.5 billion years. Uranium 235 becomes lead 207 with a half-life of about 700 million years. Nothing known in nature speeds or slows these rates. So if a mineral formed containing uranium and no lead, the ratio of lead to uranium in it today tells you how long ago it formed.
The first dates

In the first decade of the twentieth century, Ernest Rutherford and the American chemist Bertram Boltwood applied the idea. Boltwood's uranium minerals gave ages from about 400 million to more than 2 billion years, far beyond Kelvin's range. The English geologist Arthur Holmes spent decades refining the method. A difficulty remained. The Earth's surface is constantly recycled by erosion and the movement of plates, so no rock survives from the very beginning. The oldest known mineral grains, zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia, are about 4.4 billion years old.
The meteorite

The answer came from space. Meteorites are leftovers from the formation of the solar system, made at the same time as the Earth and unaltered since. In the early 1950s the American geochemist Clair Patterson set out to measure the lead in fragments of the iron meteorite that made Meteor Crater in Arizona. That meteorite contains almost no uranium, so its lead shows the mix the solar system started with. Comparing it with lead from Earth and from other meteorites gave the time elapsed. In 1956 he published the result: 4.55 billion years, give or take 70 million.
The clean room

Patterson's first measurements made no sense. His samples kept showing far too much lead. He eventually realised the lead was coming from the laboratory itself: from dust, from tools, from his own skin and hair. He spent years building one of the first ultra-clean laboratories to keep it out. The experience showed him how much lead human activity had spread through the environment, mainly from leaded petrol, and he spent much of his later career campaigning to have it removed.
Why the figure is trusted

The modern value is 4.54 billion years, with an uncertainty of about 1 percent, and it has barely moved since 1956. Its strength is agreement between independent lines. Different decay systems with different half-lives give matching ages. Many meteorites of different types cluster at the same date. The oldest rocks brought back from the Moon are a little younger, as they should be. When separate methods with separate weaknesses keep arriving at one number, the reasonable conclusion is that the number is right.
Addition is a short list of rules

Adding in binary uses the method you learned for decimal, with fewer cases. In any column, 0 plus 0 is 0. 0 plus 1 is 1. And 1 plus 1 is 2, which binary writes as 1 0, so you put down 0 and carry 1 to the next column. There are no other cases for two digits. Because the rules are so few, they can be built from logic gates, which are small circuits that take ones and zeros in and give a one or a zero out according to a fixed rule.
Two gates add one column

Look at the sum digit alone. It is 1 when exactly one of the two inputs is 1, and 0 when both are the same. That is the rule of the gate called exclusive OR, written XOR. Now look at the carry. It is 1 only when both inputs are 1, which is the rule of an AND gate. Feed the same two input bits to an XOR gate and an AND gate and you have a circuit that adds two bits. It is called a half adder, because it handles only half the job.
Handling the carry coming in

Every column except the first may also receive a carry from the column to its right, so a real adder stage needs three inputs. A full adder is built from two half adders and an OR gate. The first half adder adds the two input bits. The second adds the incoming carry to that result. If either half adder produced a carry, the OR gate passes it on. Test it with all three inputs at 1. The answer should be 3, which is 1 1 in binary. The circuit gives a sum of 1 and a carry of 1.
Chaining the stages

To add numbers of four bits, line up four full adders and connect each carry output to the carry input of the next. Add 6 and 7, which are 0 1 1 0 and 0 1 1 1. Start at the right. The first column is 0 plus 1, giving 1 and no carry. The second is 1 plus 1, giving 0 and a carry. The third is 1 plus 1 plus the carry, giving 1 and a carry. The fourth is 0 plus 0 plus the carry, giving 1. The result is 1 1 0 1, which is 13.
Why the simple adder is slow

In that chain, the last stage cannot settle until the carry has worked its way through every stage before it. The design is called a ripple-carry adder for that reason. Each stage adds a small delay, and across 64 bits those delays add up to a limit on how fast the processor can run. Faster designs, called carry-lookahead adders, use extra gates to work out in advance whether each group of columns will produce or pass on a carry. They spend more transistors to save time, which is the most common trade in chip design.
Everything from one kind of gate

A NAND gate gives 0 only when both of its inputs are 1. Any other gate can be made from NAND gates alone, which is why it is called universal. An XOR takes four of them. A complete full adder can be made from nine. In the CMOS technology used in almost all chips, a two-input NAND gate is four transistors. So one stage of this adder is 36 transistors, and a 64-bit ripple adder a little over 2,000. A modern processor has billions of transistors, most of them doing work as plain as this.
Subtraction and a bench version

A computer subtracts with the same adder. To take one number from another, it flips every bit of the second number and adds 1, a form called two's complement, and then adds as normal. Flipping is done by a row of XOR gates, and the extra 1 goes into the spare carry input of the first stage. To see all this working, the 74HC283 chip contains a complete four-bit adder. Wire eight switches to its inputs and five LEDs to its outputs on a breadboard, and you can check the sum of 6 and 7 for yourself.
Character as a craft

In the Nicomachean Ethics, written in the fourth century before Christ, Aristotle asks what makes a person good at living. His answer is that virtues are settled habits of feeling and acting well, and that they are acquired the way a skill is acquired. Nobody becomes a builder by reading about building. People become builders by building. In the same way, he says, we become just by doing just acts and brave by doing brave ones. Character is the result of what you repeatedly do.
Between too much and too little

His best-known idea is that each virtue sits between two faults, one of excess and one of deficiency. Courage lies between cowardice, which fears too much, and rashness, which fears too little. Generosity lies between meanness and wastefulness. Proper confidence lies between boasting and false modesty. Good humour lies between being a clown and being a bore. So a virtue is not the opposite of a single vice. There are two ways to miss, and the virtue is the hitting of a target between them.
The mean is not the middle

This is often mistaken for advice to be moderate in everything, and Aristotle rules that out. The right amount is relative to the person and the situation. His example is food. A quantity that is too little for a champion wrestler in training may be too much for a beginner. Likewise there is no fixed correct amount of anger. Some situations call for a great deal and some for none. The virtue is feeling and acting to the right degree, at the right time, towards the right people, for the right reason.
Why rules run out

Because the target moves with circumstances, no rule book can replace judgement. Aristotle calls the needed ability practical wisdom. It is the capacity to see what a particular situation requires, and it comes from experience. That is why he thinks the young can be brilliant at mathematics and yet rarely have it. When unsure, he suggests looking to a person of good judgement and asking what they would do. Having a real example in mind, a mentor or a grandparent, is often more useful than a principle.
Correcting your aim

He adds practical advice for people who know they tend to miss. First, of the two faults, one is usually worse, so steer away from that one. Second, notice which way you personally lean. Someone inclined to avoid conflict should aim at what feels to them like bluntness, and will probably land on honesty. He compares this to straightening a bent piece of wood by bending it the other way. Third, be wary of pleasure when judging your own case, since it bends the verdict.
A worked example

Take giving feedback to a colleague whose report is weak. The deficiency is saying nothing or offering empty praise, which protects you and fails them. The excess is listing every flaw in front of others. The mean depends on particulars. A new hire needs two main points and encouragement, in private. A senior colleague before a board meeting needs the full list today. The same honest impulse takes different forms. What stays constant is the aim, their improvement, and the question of what this person in this situation needs.
Practising it

Pick one trait you would like to strengthen. Name its two failure modes, and admit which one you usually fall into. For a month, in the situations where it arises, lean deliberately the other way and take note of what happens. Aristotle's claim is that the act comes first and the feeling follows. Doing the brave thing while afraid is how fear loosens. Over time the right response stops requiring effort and becomes what you are like. He also reminds his readers that a person is made by many days, not one.

c: Two orders of events

This piece describes United States accounts. A traditional account, such as a traditional IRA or 401(k), generally lets you put money in before income tax, grows untaxed, and is taxed as income when you withdraw. A Roth account takes money on which you have already paid tax, grows untaxed, and is generally not taxed on withdrawal in retirement if the conditions are met. One taxes the seed and the other taxes the harvest. Contribution limits, income limits and conditions change, so check the current rules or ask a tax professional before acting.
The sum that surprises people

Suppose you have 5,000 dollars of salary to set aside, pay tax at 22 percent, and the investment quadruples by retirement. In a traditional account, all 5,000 goes in and becomes 20,000. Withdraw it at 22 percent tax and you keep 15,600. In a Roth, you pay the tax first, so 3,900 goes in. It quadruples to 15,600, with no tax due. The results are identical. Paying a given rate at the start or at the end makes no difference, because multiplication gives the same answer in either order.
What actually decides it

The results differ only when the two rates differ. If your rate in retirement will be lower than today's, the traditional account wins, because you avoid tax at the high rate and pay at the low one. In the example, withdrawing at 12 percent leaves 17,600. If your rate will be higher later, the Roth wins. So the choice is a forecast about your own future income and about future tax law, and nobody knows either for certain. That uncertainty is a reason many people hold some of each.
Who tends to choose which

Some rough patterns follow. People early in a career, in a low bracket and expecting to earn more, often lean towards Roth, since they are paying tax at what may be their lowest rate. People in their peak earning years, in a high bracket, often lean towards traditional, expecting a lower income in retirement. Retirement income is often lower than working income simply because the saving stops and some costs fall away. These are tendencies, and your circumstances may not fit them.
The hidden size difference

Contribution limits are stated in dollars, and the same dollar figure applies to both types. But a dollar in a Roth is worth more than a dollar in a traditional account, because the tax on it has already been paid. Someone who puts the maximum into a Roth has sheltered more real wealth than someone who puts the same figure into a traditional account, part of which belongs to the tax authority. For savers who reach the limits, this tilts the comparison towards Roth.
Other differences

Three further points are worth knowing. If an employer matches your contributions, take the match first whichever type you choose, since it is an immediate return on your money. Rules on when the government forces withdrawals to begin have differed between the two types, which affects people who do not need the money and want to leave it growing. And a mix of both gives you a choice in retirement about which account to draw from in a given year, which can help manage your tax bill.
A way to decide

Write down your current marginal tax rate, the rate on your last dollar of income. Then make an honest estimate of your income in retirement and the rate it would attract under today's brackets. If the retirement rate is clearly lower, favour traditional. If clearly higher, favour Roth. If you cannot tell, split your contributions, which guarantees you are not entirely wrong. Review it when your income changes sharply. This is a description of how the trade-off works, not tax advice for your situation.
The wheel

An American roulette wheel has 38 pockets: the numbers 1 to 36, half red and half black, plus a green zero and a green double zero. A European wheel has 37, with a single zero. You can bet on one number, on small groups of numbers, or on large groups such as red, odd, or the first dozen. The payouts are set as if the green pockets did not exist. That gap between the true odds and the paid odds is the whole business model of the game, and it can be worked out exactly.
One number

A bet on a single number pays 35 to 1. On an American wheel there are 38 pockets, so the true odds against you are 37 to 1. Picture betting 1 dollar on the same number for 38 spins, with every pocket coming up once. You win once and collect 35, and lose the other 37 times. You are down 2 dollars on 38 dollars bet. That is a loss of 5.26 percent, or about 5 cents on each dollar wagered. It is called the house edge.
Red or black

Try the bet that feels safest. Red pays even money and covers 18 pockets. Over the same 38 spins you win 18 times and lose 20, because the two green pockets count against you. Down 2 dollars on 38 again, the same 5.26 percent. Work through dozens, columns, splits and corners and each comes to exactly the same figure. On the American wheel there is one exception, a bet on the five numbers zero, double zero, 1, 2 and 3, which pays 6 to 1 and loses 7.89 percent. Avoid that one.
One zero or two

On a European wheel the single-number bet still pays 35 to 1, but there are only 37 pockets. Over 37 spins you win 35 once and lose 36 times, down 1 dollar on 37, which is 2.70 percent. A single zero halves the cost of playing. Some tables also use a French rule on even-money bets, under which you lose only half your stake when zero comes up, bringing the edge on those bets to 1.35 percent. If you are going to play, the choice of wheel matters more than anything you do afterwards.
Why doubling up fails

The oldest system is to bet on red, double the stake after every loss, and return to the starting stake after a win, so each win recovers all losses plus one unit. Start at 10 dollars. After seven losses in a row you have lost 1,270 dollars and the next bet is 1,280, all to end up 10 ahead. Seven straight losses happen about 1.1 percent of the time on an American wheel, roughly once in every 89 sequences. Table limits and finite wallets guarantee that the long losing run arrives before the system can outlast it.
The wheel has no memory

On August 18, 1913, at the casino in Monte Carlo, black came up 26 times in a row. Players lost heavily betting on red during the run, convinced it was due. It was not. Each spin is independent of the last, and after 10 blacks the chance of red is what it always was. The belief that a streak must correct itself is known as the gambler's fallacy. No arrangement of stakes changes the edge either. Every system is a different way of dividing up the same expected loss.
What it costs

Treat the edge as a price. Multiply your average bet by the number of spins and by the edge. At 10 dollars a spin and 40 spins an hour on an American wheel, you wager 400 dollars an hour, and 5.26 percent of that is about 21 dollars. That is the average cost of an hour of entertainment, with wide swings around it on any single night. Seen that way, the sensible decisions are plain. Pick the single-zero wheel, set the amount you are willing to pay, and stop when it is spent.
